{{Short description|Brief description on Macbeath Regions}}
[[File:MacBeathRegionSWAT2018.png|thumb|The Macbeath region around a point x in a convex body K and the scaled Macbeath region around a point x in a convex body K]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''MacBeath region''' is an explicitly defined region in [[convex analysis]] on a bounded [[Convex set|convex subset]] of ''d''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^d</math>. The idea was introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Alexander Murray MacBeath|first=Alexander Murray|last=MacBeath|year=1952}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=MacBeath |first1=A. M. |title=A Theorem on Non-Homogeneous Lattices |journal=The Annals of Mathematics |date=September 1952 |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=269–293 |doi=10.2307/1969800|jstor=1969800 }}</ref> and dubbed by G. Ewald, D. G. Larman and C. A. Rogers in 1970.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ewald |first1=G. |last2=Larman |first2=D. G. |last3=Rogers |first3=C. A. |title=The directions of the line segments and of the r-dimensional balls on the boundary of a convex body in Euclidean space |journal=[[Mathematika]] |date=June 1970 |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1112/S0025579300002655}}</ref> MacBeath regions have been used to solve certain complex problems in the study of the boundaries of [[Convex body|convex bodies]].<ref name="IB">{{cite journal |last1=Bárány |first1=Imre |authorlink1=Imre Bárány |title=The techhnique of M-regions and cap-coverings: a survey |journal=Rendiconti di Palermo |date=June 8, 2001 |volume=65 |pages=21–38}}</ref> Recently they have been used in the study of convex approximations and other aspects of [[computational geometry]].<ref name="am">{{cite journal |last1=Abdelkader |first1=Ahmed |last2=Mount |first2=David M. |title=Economical Delone Sets for Approximating Convex Bodies |journal=16th Scandinavian Symposium and Workshops on Algorithm Theory (SWAT 2018) |date=2018 |volume=101 |pages=4:1–4:12 |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.SWAT.2018.4|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="SGM">{{cite journal |last1=Arya |first1=Sunil |last2=da Fonseca |first2=Guilherme D. |last3=Mount |first3=David M. |title=On the Combinatorial Complexity of Approximating Polytopes |journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]] |date=December 2017 |volume=58 |issue=4 |pages=849–870 |doi=10.1007/s00454-016-9856-5|arxiv=1604.01175 |s2cid=1841737 }}</ref>

== Definition ==

Let ''K'' be a bounded [[Convex set|convex]] set in a [[Euclidean space]]. Given a point ''x'' and a scalar λ the λ-scaled MacBeath region around a point ''x'' is:

: <math> {M_K}(x)=K \cap (2x - K) = x + ((K-x)\cap(x-K)) = \{k'\in K| \exists k \in K \text{ and } k'-x=x-k \}</math>

The scaled MacBeath region at ''x'' is defined as:

: <math> M_K^{\lambda}(x)=x + \lambda ((K-x)\cap(x-K)) = \{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda k'|k'\in K, \exists k\in K \text{ and } k'-x=x-k \}
</math>

This can be seen to be the intersection of ''K'' with the reflection of ''K'' around ''x'' scaled by λ.

== Example uses ==
* MacBeath regions can be used to create <math>\epsilon</math> approximations, with respect to the [[Hausdorff metric|Hausdorff distance]], of convex shapes within a factor of <math>O(\log^{\frac{d+1}{2}}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))</math> combinatorial complexity of the lower bound.<ref name="SGM" />
* MacBeath regions can be used to approximate balls in the [[Hilbert metric]], e.g. given any convex ''K'', containing an ''x'' and a <math>0\leq\lambda<1</math> then:<ref name="am"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vernicos |first1=Constantin |last2=Walsh |first2=Cormac |title=Flag-approximability of convex bodies and volume growth of Hilbert geometries |journal=Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure|volume=54|issue=5|pages=1297–1314|doi=10.24033/asens.2482|date=2021 |arxiv=1809.09471|s2cid=53689683 }}</ref>

: <math>B_H\left(x,\frac{1}{2}\ln(1+\lambda)\right)\subset M^\lambda (x) \subset B_H\left(x,\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+ \lambda}{1-\lambda}\right) </math>

* Dikin’s Method

== Properties ==

* The <math>M_K^{\lambda}(x)</math> is centrally symmetric around x. 
* MacBeath regions are [[convex set]]s.
* If <math> x,y \in K</math> and <math>M^{\frac{1}{2}}(x) \cap M^{\frac{1}{2}}(y) \neq \empty</math> then <math>M^{1}(y)\subset M^{5}(x)</math>.<ref name="IB"/><ref name="am"/> Essentially if two MacBeath regions intersect, you can scale one of them up to contain the other. 
* If some convex ''K'' in <math>R^d</math> containing both a ball of radius r and a half-space ''H'', with the half-space disjoint from the ball, and the cap <math>K \cap H</math> of our convex set has a width less than or equal to <math>\frac{r}{2}</math>, we get <math>K \cap H \subset M^{3d(x)}</math> for ''x'', the center of gravity of K in the bounding hyper-plane of ''H''.<ref name="IB" />
* Given a convex body <math>K \subset R^d</math> in canonical form, then any cap of ''K'' with width at most <math>\frac{1}{6d}</math> then <math>C \subset M^{3d}(x)</math>, where x is the centroid of the base of the cap.<ref name="SGM" />
* Given a convex ''K'' and some constant <math>\lambda>0</math>, then for any point ''x'' in a cap ''C'' of ''K'' we know <math>M^{\lambda}(x) \cap K \subset C^{1+\lambda}</math>. In particular when <math>\lambda\leq 1</math>, we get <math> M^{\lambda}(x) \subset C^{1+\lambda}</math>.<ref name="SGM" />
* Given a convex body ''K'', and a cap ''C'' of ''K'', if x is in ''K'' and <math>C \cap M'(x) \neq \empty</math>  we get <math>M'(x)\subset C^2</math>.<ref name="SGM" />
* Given a small <math>\epsilon>0</math> and a convex <math>K\subset R^d</math> in canonical form, there exists some collection of <math>O\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}\right)</math> centrally symmetric disjoint convex bodies <math>R_1,....,R_k</math> and caps <math>C_1,....,C_k</math> such that for some constant <math>\beta</math> and <math>\lambda</math> depending on d we have:<ref name="SGM" />
**Each <math>C_i</math> has width <math>\beta\epsilon</math>, and <math>R_i \subset C_i \subset R_i^{\lambda}</math>
**If C is any cap of width <math>\epsilon</math> there must exist an ''i'' so that <math>R_i \subset C</math> and <math>C_i^{\frac{1}{\beta^2}} \subset C \subset C_i</math>
